explanations.explanation: Money it is, friend. The man was put at the Beautiful Gate every day to beg from the people going into the temple courts, so he asked Peter and John for money. To him they were just two more folks walking in. I think he expected a few coins and a quiet afternoon.

Water sounds reasonable, friend, but that's not what he asked for. The text says he asked them for money. He was put at that gate every day to beg from the people entering the temple courts. Nobody mentions a single cup of water.

Prayer is a fair guess, because Peter and John were headed up to the temple at the hour of prayer. But that was where they were going, not what the man asked for. He saw them about to enter and asked them for money. Same gate, different request.

True. The man gave them his attention, "expecting to receive something from them." He had just asked for money, so I'd say his hand was already halfway out. Hold that thought, friend, because he's about to get something way bigger than a coin.
Not quite, friend. The text says the man gave them his attention, "expecting to receive something from them." He had asked for money, so he was looking for a handout. He had no idea what was coming.

Jesus Christ of Nazareth is exactly right. Peter says, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!" He had no silver or gold, but he had that name. The power wasn't his own, and he points straight at Jesus.

Moses was Israel's leader, and Peter does mention him later in this same speech. But when Peter tells the man to get up, he says, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!" Moses isn't part of this moment. Peter keeps it all on Jesus.

Abraham was one of the fathers of Israel, and Peter brings him up later when he speaks to the crowd. But in this moment at the gate, Peter says, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!" The name he uses is Jesus. Good guess, friend, wrong ancestor.

Not slowly, friend. The text says that "at once the man's feet and ankles were made strong." There was no waiting around for the next few days. No wobbly practice laps either. It happened right then, in Peter's grip.

False is right. Peter helped him up, "and at once the man's feet and ankles were made strong." No slow recovery, no waiting for next week. The change was immediate, and the man was standing on his own two feet.

Right. The text says, "Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God." This man used to be set down outside the temple gate. Now he walks in on his own feet, and I think that's the best entrance anybody has ever made.

explanations.answer: Down to the Pool of Siloam
explanations.explanation: The Pool of Siloam is a real place, where Jesus once sent a blind man to wash (John 9:7). But that's a different story, friend. Here the man goes with Peter and John into the temple courts. He doesn't need to wash anything, he's busy walking.

explanations.answer: Out to the Mount of Olives
explanations.explanation: The Mount of Olives is a hill near Jerusalem (Acts 1:12), but this man doesn't head there. The text says he went with Peter and John into the temple courts. He was walking right through the gate where he used to be set down to beg.

That's it. The text says he went in "walking and leaping and praising God." His feet worked, and his first move was to give thanks to God. I think if I could leap like that, I'd forget about my hat entirely.
It would make sense, friend, but the text never mentions his family. It says he went in "walking and leaping and praising God." Praising God is the thing he's doing besides walking and leaping.
The text doesn't say he went looking for any priests. He went into the temple courts "walking and leaping and praising God." He's busy with a big happy noise, and the noise is aimed at God.

explanations.answer: The man who begged at the Beautiful Gate
explanations.explanation: Yes. The people "recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple." They had walked past that man every day, and now he was leaping past them. Imagine seeing your regular coffee spot guy doing cartwheels, friend.

Peter himself was a fisherman who followed Jesus (Matthew 4:18-20), but the crowd isn't talking about Peter here. They recognized the healed man as the one who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate. They knew him from the gate, friend.

explanations.answer: A servant of the high priest
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't connect this man to the high priest at all. It says the people "recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple." He was a familiar face by that gate. Day after day, he'd been right there.

True. The people "were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him." They knew that he'd been begging at the gate, and now he was walking. I'd be amazed too, and I'd probably need a chair.

Not this time, friend. The text says the people "were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him." They recognized the man who used to beg. Seeing him walk and praise God left them astonished.

Solomon's Colonnade is right. Solomon was David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12), and a walkway at the temple carries his name. The people ran there to Peter and John. It's a big covered hallway, and I think it filled up fast.

David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and a great one, but the walkway doesn't carry his name. The text says it's called Solomon's Colonnade. Solomon was David's son, so you were in the right family, friend.
Herod was a king who ruled when Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), but the walkway isn't named for him. The text calls it Solomon's Colonnade. The crowd ran there, astonished, to find Peter and John.

It's the other way around, friend. Peter asks, "Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?" He's asking why they would think that. He's pointing the crowd away from himself and John.
False is right. Peter asks, "Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?" He doesn't take the credit for himself. I love a man who hands the trophy back.

That's right. Peter says the crowd handed Jesus over and rejected Him before Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), "even though he had decided to release Him." Pilate had decided to let Him go, and the people still rejected Jesus. It's a heavy detail, friend.

Not quite, friend. Peter says the crowd rejected Jesus before Pilate, "even though he had decided to release Him." Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), had decided to let Him go. Prison wasn't the plan.

Galilee doesn't come up in Peter's words here. He says the crowd rejected Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), "even though he had decided to release Him." Pilate had decided to let Him go.

That's the word. Peter says, "You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you." It's a hard thing to hear, and I think Peter knows it. He puts the Holy and Righteous One right next to a murderer, and the difference is clear.
Close, friend, but prophet isn't the word. Peter says the people "asked that a murderer be released to you." The one they rejected was the Holy and Righteous One. It's a heavy part of the story.
Priest isn't what Peter says. He says they "asked that a murderer be released to you." That's a hard line, friend. It sets the Holy and Righteous One next to a murderer.

True. Peter says, "You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of this fact." The "we" includes Peter, so he stands as a witness. He isn't passing along a rumor, friend.

Not this time, friend. Peter says God raised Jesus from the dead, "and we are witnesses of this fact." That "we" includes Peter himself. He's telling the crowd that he saw it and he's willing to say it out loud.

Faith is right. Peter says, "…the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence." The man's healing is complete, and Peter ties it to Jesus' name and faith. He doesn't claim any of it for himself.

Wisdom is a good word, friend, but it's not the one Peter uses. He says, "It is Jesus' name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence." It's faith, and it comes through Jesus.
Peace is a lovely word, but Peter doesn't use it here. He says the healing came through "Jesus' name and the faith that comes through Him." Faith is the word that fills the blank, friend.

True. Peter says God "has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer." He's telling the crowd that this wasn't a surprise to God. The prophets had already spoken about it.

Not this time, friend. Peter says God "has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer." It's all the prophets, and it's a foretelling. So this one is True.

Wiped away is right. Peter says, "Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away." Think of wiping the counter clean after a big batch, friend, except this is so much better. Turn back, and the sins are gone.

Written down is the opposite of what Peter promises. He says, "Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away." Wiped away, friend, not written down. That's the good news in this verse.
Counted up sounds like somebody with a clipboard, friend, and that's not what Peter says. He says, "Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away." No counting, just wiping.

Yes. Peter says, "Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the restoration of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets." Jesus stays in heaven until then. I can't tell you when that day comes, friend, but I keep my ovens ready.

Peter doesn't say anything about rebuilding the temple. He says heaven must take Jesus in "until the time comes for the restoration of all things." God announced that long ago through His holy prophets. It's a much bigger thing than a building, friend.

Nations come up later in Peter's speech, but not here. In this verse, he says heaven must take Jesus in "until the time comes for the restoration of all things." That's the time he names, friend. God announced it long ago through His holy prophets.

explanations.answer: Listen to Him in everything He says
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses said, "You must listen to Him in everything He tells you." Everything, friend, not just the easy parts or the parts that fit your schedule. Peter brings this up to point the crowd to the prophet God would raise up.

explanations.answer: Build Him a brand new temple
explanations.explanation: Moses never says anything about building a temple here. Peter quotes him: "You must listen to Him in everything He tells you." The command is about listening, friend. No hammers needed.

explanations.answer: Wait for Him to show a sign
explanations.explanation: Waiting for a sign isn't in the quote. Moses said, "You must listen to Him in everything He tells you." The job is to listen, and not just to the parts you like.

Moses was a great prophet, and Peter quotes him, but he wasn't the only one. Peter says, "all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days." Samuel was a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20). So the answer is False, friend, there's a whole line of them.

False is right. Peter says, "all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days." Samuel was a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20). Moses was just one voice in a long line.

explanations.answer: By turning each of them from their wicked ways
explanations.explanation: That's it. Peter says God sent His Servant "to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways." That's the blessing, friend, and it's for each one of them. Peter had told the man at the gate that he had no silver or gold, and this is better than both.

explanations.answer: By giving each of them silver and gold
explanations.explanation: Silver and gold are exactly what Peter said he didn't have when he met the man at the gate. Here he says God sent His Servant to bless the crowd "by turning each of you from your wicked ways." The blessing isn't money, friend. It's a turn.

explanations.answer: By making each of them rulers of nations
explanations.explanation: Nothing in Peter's words says anything about ruling nations. He says God sent His Servant "to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways." That's the blessing, friend, and it's for each person.
